OpenVLHarness: Real World Visual Agentic Tool-Use with Multimodal Memory

Yu Zhou Affiliation: University of California, Los Angeles    Cheng-Fu Yang Affiliation: University of California, Los Angeles    Rui Sun Affiliation: University of California, Los Angeles    Di Wu Affiliation: University of California, Los Angeles    Sibo Peng Affiliation: University of California, Los Angeles    Mingyang Zhang Affiliation: University of California, Los Angeles    Zhen Yang Affiliation: Apple*Equal contributionProject page: openvlharness.github.ioCode: github.com/uclanlp/OpenVLHarness    Ruiyi Zhang Affiliation: Apple*Equal contributionProject page: openvlharness.github.ioCode: github.com/uclanlp/OpenVLHarness    Nanyun Peng Affiliation: University of California, Los Angeles    Zhe Gan Affiliation: Apple*Equal contributionProject page: openvlharness.github.ioCode: github.com/uclanlp/OpenVLHarness    Kai-Wei Chang Affiliation: University of California, Los Angeles
Abstract

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made rapid progress on visual reasoning, yet many tasks require evidence that is difficult to obtain through internal reasoning alone: our controlled study on 22 benchmarks shows that simply increasing the inference budget of the base model yields only modest gains. Such tasks demand grounded perception, external knowledge, and numerical measurements obtained through heterogeneous tools, whose outputs must be made interpretable to the model and retained across reasoning steps. We introduce OpenVLHarness, a multimodal reasoning harness organized around a capability layer and persistent multimodal memory. The capability layer combines task-level tool interfaces with evidence rendering, providing consistent access to heterogeneous backends and converting their outputs into model-readable observations. Persistent multimodal memory retains the corresponding images, structured data, and web references as addressable artifacts throughout each query. A coding interface executes generated programs over stored data, enabling computations that combine results from multiple tools. Together, these mechanisms support an iterative process of acquiring, inspecting, and composing multimodal evidence. Evaluated on 22 benchmarks with eight open and proprietary backbones, OpenVLHarness improves average scores by 9.7–12.6 points over matched no-tool baselines, including +11.2 with Qwen3-VL-8B, +9.7 with Kimi K3, and +9.9 with GPT-6 Astra. With GPT-6 Luna at medium reasoning effort, OpenVLHarness outperforms the base model, Codex, and Visual Sketchpad at maximum effort by 7.7–8.5 points while incurring at most 37% of their model-token cost.

1 Introduction

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used as reasoning engines over images, documents, webpages, and videos. However, many real-world visual tasks require information that the model cannot reliably infer from the input alone. Answering a question may require localizing numerous tiny objects in dense scenes, retrieving external knowledge about a long-tail entity, or computing quantities from intermediate measurements. Such tasks require additional multimodal evidence acquired through perception, search, and computation. Our inference-time scaling study (Fig. 1c) reveals diminishing returns at higher reasoning budgets: moving the base model from xhigh to max effort multiplies its model-token spending by 2.7 but improves its average score by only 0.7 points. This raises the question of whether further progress requires better access to task-relevant multimodal evidence, beyond additional reasoning over the initial input.

Visual tool-use agents address this need by connecting MLLMs to perception models, search engines, and code execution (Hong et al., 2026a; Wu et al., 2025a; Narayan et al., 2025; Geng et al., 2026; Su et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025b; Surís et al., 2023; Gupta and Kembhavi, 2023). Building a general harness around these tools presents two connected challenges. First, heterogeneous backends expose different calling conventions and return outputs such as segmentation masks, depth maps, and retrieved webpages that need to be presented in a form the model can interpret. Second, subsequent reasoning steps may still need access to the underlying artifacts: a rendered depth map supports visual inspection, but a precise measurement requires its numerical values. Effective multimodal tool use therefore requires both consistent tool interfaces with evidence rendering and a mechanism for retaining and reusing the resulting artifacts.

We introduce OpenVLHarness, a multimodal reasoning harness organized around a capability layer and persistent multimodal memory. The capability layer combines task-level tool interfaces with model-facing evidence rendering. Task-level interfaces define operations independently of a particular backend, allowing tools to be replaced without changing the orchestrator’s task vocabulary. Evidence rendering converts heterogeneous outputs into observations that combine visualizations, concise descriptions, and compact structured information. For example, visual grounding accepts an image and a textual query, then presents the detected regions through an annotated image and coordinates. Together, these mechanisms let the orchestrator invoke tools consistently and inspect their results in a form suited to multimodal reasoning.

Persistent multimodal memory makes the corresponding artifacts available across turns within a query. Images, structured data, and web references are registered under reusable handles, allowing later calls to operate on earlier evidence. In the grounding example, the orchestrator can inspect the overlay, then reuse the retained masks and a subsequently acquired depth array to measure depth within each region. A Python Coding Agent supports such compositions: the orchestrator specifies a computational objective in natural language, and a code-generation session backed by the same backbone model writes a program that executes over the stored data. The capability layer makes tool results interpretable; memory makes their underlying artifacts addressable and reusable. Together, they support an iterative process of acquiring, inspecting, and computing over multimodal evidence.

We evaluate OpenVLHarness on 22 benchmarks spanning grounded perception, visual search and deep research, general VQA and hallucination, and spatial reasoning, using eight open and proprietary MLLM backbones of different scales (Fig. 1a). Across these settings, OpenVLHarness consistently improves average performance over the base MLLMs by 9.7–12.6 percentage points and outperforms existing visual tool-use baselines (Fig. 1c). Scaling experiments on 22 benchmarks further show that OpenVLHarness also benefits from greater reasoning effort (Fig. 1c), suggesting that evidence acquisition and inference-time scaling are complementary. We conduct ablation studies to examine the incremental effects of the capability layer and memory, showing the value of both usable tool outputs and retained multimodal artifacts. Lastly, for users who would like to adapt our harness to a custom domain, we further showcase two coding-agent-driven workflows for specialization: harness search edits prompts, tool descriptions, and output templates, while tool generation composes existing capabilities into new tools. Both operate without updating the underlying MLLM weights.

Our contributions are: (1) a capability layer that combines task-level tool interfaces with model-facing evidence rendering for heterogeneous perception, search, and computation tools; (2) persistent multimodal memory that retains addressable artifacts across turns and enables their reuse in subsequent tool calls and memory-grounded computation; and (3) an evaluation across 22 benchmarks and eight backbones, with component ablations and domain-specialization studies, accompanied by an open-source release of the harness, tools, evaluation protocols, and two optimization workflows.

2 Harness Design

OpenVLHarness augments an MLLM orchestrator with two complementary mechanisms (Figure 2). The capability layer combines task-level tool interfaces with model-facing evidence rendering, providing consistent access to tools and observations the orchestrator can inspect (Sec. 2.1). Persistent multimodal memory retains the corresponding artifacts and exposes them by reference for reuse across turns within a query (Sec. 2.2). At each step, the orchestrator uses the observations and available memory references to select a tool call or produce an answer. A Python Coding Agent supports computation over stored artifacts, connecting outputs from different capabilities into multi-step procedures. The modular interfaces and renderers also support harness specialization through text edits and tool composition (Sec. 3.6).

2.1 Capability Layer

We design the capability layer with two goals: defining how the orchestrator invokes a capability and rendering the resulting evidence for inspection. The first accommodates different backends behind a consistent interface; the second addresses the heterogeneous formats of their outputs.

Task-level tool interfaces.

We define a capability by the operation it provides, its typed inputs, and the evidence and reusable data it exposes. For example, visual grounding accepts an image reference and a textual query and exposes object locations, associated metadata, and a visualization; a supporting backend may additionally provide segmentation masks. Each backend is wrapped to implement this task-level interface. Visual Grounding can thus use SAM 3 or Grounding DINO, and OCR can use PaddleOCR-VL or DeepSeek-OCR, while preserving the orchestrator’s calling convention (Appendix C). Backend selection can reflect accuracy, cost, and latency requirements. Our base instantiation includes nine capabilities: five for perception—Zoom-in, Visual Grounding, OCR, Depth Estimation, and Camera Trajectory; three for information seeking—Text Search, Image Search, and Webpage Visit; and a Python Coding Agent for computation over intermediate results. Please refer to Appendix C and Table 18 for their implementation details.

Model-facing evidence rendering.

Raw tool outputs often require additional processing to become useful observations. An RLE mask encodes a region precisely, but serializing that encoding into the context does not show the orchestrator which object was segmented. Dense numerical arrays can likewise consume substantial context without providing useful, interpretable evidence.

Each capability therefore includes an output processor that renders its result into a model-facing observation. Depending on the capability, this observation combines visual attachments, concise natural-language descriptions, compact structured information, and references to reusable artifacts. Grounding can return a labeled mask overlay with the number of detected objects and normalized bounding boxes; depth estimation can return a colorized map; and Camera Trajectory can return a visualization of the recovered trajectory. The underlying masks, arrays, and camera parameters are passed to memory for later reuse. Figure 2 illustrates grounding for “cabinet” in input_image_3. The capability returns a mask overlay with a description of the five grounded objects and their bounding boxes, allowing the orchestrator to inspect the detections. If a subsequent step requires a depth measurement for each cabinet, this rendered observation supplies the visual context, while the retained masks and a depth array supply the data for computation. The memory mechanism below connects these steps.

2.2 Persistent Multimodal Memory

The capability layer makes tool results interpretable; persistent multimodal memory makes their underlying artifacts addressable and reusable. A later tool call must be able to identify a particular image, mask, or array and access its contents. Repeating a description of a previous result does not provide this access.

We maintain an explicit artifact registry for each query, with entries retained across its reasoning trajectory. The registry separates an artifact’s payload from the handle used to reference it. The orchestrator sees available names and compact descriptors, while the harness retains the underlying values and resolves references when needed. The registry contains three categories:

  • •

    Image artifacts: input, tool-generated, and retrieved images, exposed through handles such as input_image_3 and tool_generated_image_6. Duplicate images reuse an existing registry entry.

  • •

    Structured data bindings: named values containing boxes, scores, masks, depth arrays, camera parameters, OCR results, and other tool outputs. Each binding has a descriptor identifying its fields and types, including array shapes where applicable.

  • •

    Web references: retrieved URLs exposed through handles such as webpage_url_1, allowing later navigation without requiring the model to reproduce the original URL.

Registering and reusing artifacts.

After a successful tool call, the harness registers supported artifacts and associates their handles with the capability’s rendered observation. Images are delivered as visual attachments with named references; structured payloads remain accessible through data bindings. An Environment Update advertises the available image handles, data bindings, and web references after each tool turn, exposing the current namespace without repeating every artifact’s full payload. In the cabinet example, the grounding call adds an overlay image and bindings for the detection data, including bounding boxes and RLE masks.

When a subsequent call refers to an artifact, the harness resolves its handle to the input required by the receiving tool. An image handle supplies the image for a later visual operation, a web reference supplies a URL for Webpage Visit, and a data binding supplies values for code execution. The orchestrator can thus reuse the grounding and depth results without reconstructing their contents from earlier descriptions. References connect retained evidence across tools and turns. The detailed representation and handles can be found in Appendix C.4 and Table 19.

Memory-grounded computation.

To compute depth within the detected cabinets, the orchestrator delegates a natural-language objective to the Python Coding Agent, such as “compute the average depth within each detected region.” The harness supplies descriptors of the available memory bindings to a fresh code-generation context of the same backbone model. The generated program executes with the actual binding values available as named variables, allowing it to combine the grounding masks with the depth array. Execution results and feedback return in language, with supported output artifacts registered for subsequent reuse. The orchestrator can then use the result or revise the objective in a later call.

This mechanism also supports filtering detections, aggregating OCR values, and other computations over intermediate results without requiring the orchestrator to serialize large arrays into its request. The capability layer supplies reusable operations and interpretable observations; memory and code execution connect their outputs into longer reasoning procedures.

Qualitative examples.

Figure 3 shows three trajectories from our evaluation. In each, the agent chains several capabilities and reuses their outputs through memory: camera poses, depth maps, and grounding masks become bindings for exact 3D computation (a); grounded crops are passed by identifier to zoom-in, OCR, and image search before the answer is verified on the web (b); and masks from two grounding queries are reconciled in code to correct an undercount (c).

3 Experiments

3.1 Tasks, Models, and Baselines

Tasks.

We evaluate OpenVLHarness across four task domains spanning 22 datasets, as summarized in Table 1 (splits, sizes, and scoring in Appendix D):

  • •

    Grounded perception. Five benchmarks targeting object counting and open-vocabulary visual grounding: CountQA (Tamarapalli et al., 2025), FSC-147 (Ranjan et al., 2021), OdinW-13-All (Li et al., 2022), FSCD-147 (Nguyen et al., 2022), and FSCD-LVIS (Nguyen et al., 2022).

  • •

    Visual search and deep research. Six benchmarks drawn from a suite of 11 multimodal information-seeking tasks: FVQA (Wu et al., 2025a), MMSearch (Jiang et al., 2024), MMSearch-Plus (Tao et al., 2026), HLE-VL (Phan et al., 2025), BrowseComp-VL (Geng et al., 2026), and RealX-Bench (Hong et al., 2026a); the remaining five are evaluated in Appendix B.5.

  • •

    General VQA and hallucination. Six benchmarks covering general visual question answering and hallucination robustness: RealWorldQA (xAI, 2024), SimpleVQA (Cheng et al., 2025), HallusionBench (Guan et al., 2024), FREAK-VQA (Yin et al., 2026), FREAK-MCQ (Yin et al., 2026), and V* (Wu and Xie, 2024).

  • •

    Spatial reasoning. Five benchmarks targeting spatial and embodied reasoning: MMSI-Bench (Yang et al., 2025b), ERQA (Team et al., 2025), EmbSpatial-Bench (Du et al., 2024), SparBench (Zhang et al., 2026a), and MindCube (Wang et al., 2025c).

Models and baselines.

We instantiate OpenVLHarness on four open-source models across different sizes—Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct (Qwen Team, 2025a), Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (Qwen Team, 2025b), Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct, and Kimi K3 (Team et al., 2026)—and four proprietary models: GPT-5 (OpenAI, 2025b), GPT-6 Luna, GPT-6 Sol, and GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI, 2026). Per-model sampling parameters can be found in Appendix C.6. Because the search APIs, the agent’s tool-routing decisions, and the LLM judge are all stochastic, every Qwen3-VL result, for OpenVLHarness and for all baselines, is the mean of three independent runs with different random seeds, while results with proprietary backbones are single runs because of API cost (standard deviations in Appendix H). In addition to the no-tool baseline (denoted Base), we compare OpenVLHarness against two groups of baselines: Training-based baselines: AdaReasoner (Song et al., 2026), PixelReasoner (Wang et al., 2025a), and DeepEyesV2 (Hong et al., 2026a)—harnesses that require fine-tuning the backbone to adapt it to the tool-use framework—evaluated with their released Qwen2.5-VL-7B checkpoints (Appendix Table 9; setup in Appendix G.2). Training-free baselines: Visual Sketchpad (Hu et al., 2024) and OctoTools (Lu et al., 2025) are visual tool-use harnesses evaluated on the same Qwen3-VL backbones as OpenVLHarness (detailed setup in Appendix G.1). We additionally evaluate Visual Sketchpad and Codex on GPT-6 Luna.

3.2 Main Results

Across the evaluated backbones, OpenVLHarness improves average performance over the underlying base model and outperforms all existing training-free harnesses (Table 1). On Qwen3-VL-8B, it raises the 22-dataset average from 34.234.2 to 45.445.4 (+11.2+11.2), exceeding the strongest training-free baseline, OctoTools (31.831.8), by 13.613.6 points; on Qwen3-VL-32B, the average rises from 38.338.3 to 50.950.9 (+12.6+12.6). The gains extend to GPT-5 (→55.744.4\!\to\!55.7), GPT-6 Sol (→64.352.7\!\to\!64.3), and Kimi K3 (→66.156.4\!\to\!66.1) (Appendix Table 7). On the Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbone, OpenVLHarness averages 33.4533.45 across the 22 datasets, surpassing the training-based baselines AdaReasoner (25.2925.29), PixelReasoner (28.0228.02), and DeepEyesV2 (25.0225.02), without updating model weights (Appendix Table 9).

The GPT-6 results highlight that effective multimodal tool use depends on the harness. With GPT-6 Luna, Codex averages 43.843.8, below the no-tool baseline (45.845.8), while OpenVLHarness reaches 56.556.5. This comparison shows that a coding-agent harness does not automatically improve multimodal reasoning. With GPT-6 Astra, OpenVLHarness improves all 22 benchmarks and raises the average from 60.360.3 to 70.270.2, the highest of any backbone.

Grounded perception and visual search and deep research benefit substantially from dedicated vision experts and external retrieval, respectively. Gains on general VQA and hallucination and on spatial reasoning depend more on the backbone: Luna and Astra improve on every benchmark in these domains (Luna by less than one point on RealWorldQA, HallusionBench, and EmbSpatial), with average gains of +6.5+6.5/+7.5+7.5 on general VQA and hallucination and +6.5+6.5/+5.2+5.2 on spatial reasoning, respectively. This pattern is consistent with greater proficiency in using tools and reasoning over their visual evidence. The less consistent gains on Qwen3-VL-8B motivate the failure analysis and domain specialization in Secs. 3.5 and 3.6.

3.3 Can More Reasoning Replace the Harness?

OpenVLHarness makes several model calls per question, each carrying tool outputs and memory, so it spends more model tokens than prompting the base model directly. To test whether its gains come simply from extra computation, we run Base, Codex, Visual Sketchpad, and OpenVLHarness with GPT-6 Luna at five reasoning-effort settings, from low to max, on the full evaluation splits of all 22 benchmarks (26,22926{,}229 questions per setting). Figure 1c reports the 22-benchmark averages against model-token cost, and Table 2 breaks them down by domain.

Additional effort yields limited gains for the other methods: from low to max effort, Base rises from 44.3 to 48.0 and Visual Sketchpad from 44.7 to 48.8, while Codex, the weakest method at low effort, rises from 36.9 to 48.6. The step from xhigh to max effort alone multiplies their model-token cost by 1.5–2.7. At max effort, all three remain well below OpenVLHarness at medium effort (56.5), which spends at most 37% of their model-token cost per question, and OpenVLHarness at low effort (49.9) is already on par with their max-effort averages. The domain breakdown shows where the harness matters most. On grounded perception and on visual search and deep research, every effort setting of OpenVLHarness, including low, scores above every setting of the other methods, and at max effort it leads the best of them by 15.6 and 12.4 points. On general VQA and hallucination and on spatial reasoning, the harness benefits from more reasoning: at low effort, OpenVLHarness trails Base slightly (61.5 vs. 61.6 and 54.5 vs. 56.5), but from medium effort onward it scores above every setting of every other method in every domain, and at max effort it leads by 6.1 and 7.1 points. Raising the effort of OpenVLHarness itself lifts its average from 56.5 to 60.1. Acquiring and composing multimodal evidence therefore complements stronger reasoning: additional computation remains useful, but does not eliminate the benefit of the harness within the tested budgets. Costs cover model tokens, including reasoning tokens, and exclude tool execution and judging; Appendix B.6 gives the setup, per-benchmark scores, token usage, and how often Codex executes code.

3.4 Ablation Study

Table 3 examines the two mechanisms introduced in Sec. 2: the capability layer, which combines task-level tool interfaces with model-facing evidence rendering, followed by persistent multimodal memory, which makes the resulting artifacts addressable and reusable across turns. Starting from the no-tool baseline, we add raw tool access, then the capability layer, and finally memory, using a textual-memory variant as an intermediate comparison (details in Appendix B.2).

Raw tool access raises the overall average by +3.8+3.8 points at 8B and +4.3+4.3 at 32B, with the largest gains in grounded perception. Adding the capability layer restores full tool schemas and renders heterogeneous outputs into concise observations, yielding another +3.4+3.4 and +3.2+3.2 points. These gains support the joint value of task-level tool interfaces and model-facing evidence rendering; the comparison does not separate their individual contributions.

Adding textual memory enables structured data bindings, web references, and Environment Updates, but represents tool-generated images only through descriptions, without reusable image handles. This adds +0.7+0.7 points at 8B and +0.3+0.3 at 32B. Completing persistent multimodal memory with visual attachments and reusable image handles adds a further +3.1+3.1 and +4.5+4.5, bringing the full harness to 47.147.1 and 52.552.5. The largest gains from this final step occur in visual search and deep research (+6.2+6.2/+3.5+3.5), with additional gains in spatial reasoning (+2.8+2.8/+3.1+3.1). The results support the method’s complementary mechanisms: interpretable tool observations, followed by retained multimodal artifacts that can be revisited and composed across turns.

3.5 Failure Analysis

We use Kimi K3 to critique 9,8939{,}893 failed Qwen3-VL-8B trajectories across 22 benchmarks. Given the question, answer, images, trajectory, and toolbox, the critic assesses each tool call and identifies the trajectory’s primary failure cause and proposes a fix. Its labels agree with human annotations on 92%92\% of 100 sampled failures. The protocol, coverage, and taxonomy are detailed in Appendix E.1.

Surprisingly, we find that failure patterns differ across domains (Fig. 4a). Despite substantial overall gains, grounded perception remains challenging in crowded images with more than 25 objects, where missed or merged instances limit exhaustive detection. Such perception errors account for the dominant “incorrect tool output” category (75%75\% of failures in this domain). Failures in visual search and deep research most often involve an omitted tool call (49%49\%), while failures in spatial reasoning and in general VQA and hallucination involve both omitted tool calls and reasoning errors, consistent with our hypothesis that the model has limited proficiency in spatial reasoning and tool use. Failures involving unusable or ignored correct tool outputs are uncommon (33–8%8\% across domains), suggesting that the capability layer generally presents retrieved evidence in a usable form.

Failure causes alone do not determine how to specialize the harness: an omitted call may require clearer instructions or a new composition of tools. We therefore combine the cause and proposed fix into remedy channels (Fig. 4b). Constructing new task-specific tools can make evidence interpretation explicit (A), enforce systematic verification, filtering of tool results (B), or supply a missing tool composition (C). In contrast, harness text changes (Y)—edits to the system prompt, tool descriptions, and output messages—guide the model to call existing tools when needed and use their results appropriately. The remaining channel (Z) covers cases without a proposed remedy. These diagnostic recommendations guide optimization rather than predict recoverable accuracy, since the critique covers only failed trajectories. Exact mapping rules and per-dataset shares are in Appendix E.2.

3.6 Harness Optimization

When adapting OpenVLHarness to a custom domain, users can use failures on their own data to identify which parts of the harness need refinement. We provide two coding-agent-driven workflows for specializing the general-purpose harness without updating model weights. Harness search edits system prompts, tool descriptions, and evidence-rendering templates, selecting candidates through repeated evaluation. Tool generation implements and refines task-specific tools by composing existing capabilities (algorithms in Appendix E.3). To compare them, we select four datasets with contrasting remedy profiles (Fig. 4c): harness text changes (Y) dominate ERQA (71%71\%) and RealWorldQA (56%56\%), whereas task-specific tools (A+B+C) dominate SparBench (75%75\%) and FREAK-VQA (62%62\%). We run both workflows on all four datasets with Qwen3-VL-8B, testing whether their relative benefits align with these profiles.

The results follow this distinction (Fig. 4d). Harness search improves ERQA and RealWorldQA by +4.1+4.1 and +3.7+3.7 points, compared with +0.2+0.2 and +0.1+0.1 from tool generation. Conversely, tool generation improves SparBench and FREAK-VQA by +8.2+8.2 and +4.5+4.5, while harness search yields −0.5-0.5 and −1.0-1.0. The generated tools compute metric 3D relations on SparBench and make visibility decisions explicit on FREAK-VQA, matching the missing-composition and evidence-interpretation needs identified by the critique (Table 24). These results suggest a practical approach to adaptation on custom data: diagnose the prevailing failures, then use harness search to improve the use of existing capabilities or tool generation to add the task-specific operations the domain requires.

4 Related Work

Visual Tool-Use Baselines.

Early visual tool-use work treats the problem as program synthesis, compiling a question into a sequential plan that invokes vision tools in a pipeline to produce an answer (Surís et al., 2023; Gupta and Kembhavi, 2023; Kamali and Kordjamshidi, 2026; Zhao et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2023b; Gao et al., 2023; Castrejon et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026b; Zhou et al., 2024; Menon et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024b; You et al., 2023); because these plans are fixed in place, they cannot be adjusted based on tool execution results. A later line adopts multi-turn frameworks that interleave reasoning with visual feedback, but depends on brittle, task-specific framework designs that require extensive training to work (Ma et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025a; Song et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025a; Zheng et al., 2025; Hong et al., 2026a; Su et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025b; Zhao et al., 2026), and many domain-specific visual tool-use frameworks fall into the same category (Chen et al., 2025a; Wu et al., 2025a; Narayan et al., 2025; Geng et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; Du et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025d). Closest to our setting, Visual Sketchpad (Hu et al., 2024) and OctoTools (Lu et al., 2025) are training-free tool-use frameworks built around manually designed tool interfaces and execution strategies. In contrast, we focus on making the harness itself more adaptable, so its evidence processing and tool composition can be specialized as tools, MLLMs, and target tasks evolve.

Working Memory for Tool-Using Agents.

Language agents maintain intermediate information to support reasoning and action across multiple steps. Context management approaches further separate compact model-visible state from more detailed external information, enabling the agent to selectively recover relevant content when needed (Packer et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2024). Tool-using agents have also introduced explicit mechanisms for passing intermediate results across actions. ReWOO (Xu et al., 2023) represents tool evidence through referenceable variables, while CodeAct (Wang et al., 2024a) maintains intermediate results as variables in an executable interpreter. HuggingGPT (Shen et al., 2023) and LLMCompiler (Kim et al., 2024) go further in using symbolic references to intermediate tool outputs that are resolved when executing dependent downstream calls. Building on these ideas, OpenVLHarness extends them to the multimodal setting, maintaining a unified registry of typed artifacts spanning images, structured data, and web evidence. It exposes compact model-facing handles while preserving the underlying artifacts for later inspection, composition, and reuse through modality-appropriate downstream tools.

5 Conclusion

We presented OpenVLHarness, a general harness for real-world visual agentic tool use built around a capability layer and persistent multimodal memory. The capability layer combines task-level tool interfaces with evidence rendering, enabling the orchestrator to invoke heterogeneous tools and inspect their outputs. Persistent multimodal memory retains the corresponding artifacts for reuse across turns, including computation over stored data through a Python Coding Agent. Together, these mechanisms support reasoning that acquires and composes multimodal evidence. Evaluation across 22 benchmarks and eight backbones demonstrates broad gains, while component ablations show the incremental benefits of the capability layer and multimodal memory. Harness search and tool generation further specialize the system on selected domains without updating the underlying MLLM weights. We release the harness, tools, evaluation protocols, and optimization workflows to support further work on multimodal tool-use agents.

Appendix

Appendix A Tool-Use Behavior

Table 1 reports the accuracy of OpenVLHarness. This section characterizes the behavior that produces it: how frequently the agent invokes a tool, which capabilities it invokes, and how those invocations relate to accuracy relative to the same model without tools. The analysis covers five base models — Qwen3-VL-8B, Qwen3-VL-32B, GPT-6 Luna, GPT-6 Sol, and GPT-6 Astra, the GPT-6 models at medium reasoning effort — and reads every rollout of the OpenVLHarness runs behind Tables 1 and 7, approximately 123,000123{,}000 rollouts containing 224,000224{,}000 tool calls. All counts are exact rather than sampled. A question is engaged if the agent emitted at least one tool call on it, regardless of whether the call succeeded.

Measurement protocol.

Section A.3 compares OpenVLHarness against the Base columns of Tables 1 and 7 on a per-question basis: both arms answer the same questions and are scored with the same dataset metric, and differences are averaged over paired rows. This design supports statements about individual capabilities, since the rows on which a given tool was invoked can be isolated and both arms evaluated on that subset. The resulting quantities are correlational rather than causal: the agent selects the rows on which it invokes a tool, and the remaining capabilities are available on those rows as well. Each per-tool measurement is therefore reported alongside a control, namely the same paired difference computed on the rows that did not invoke the tool. A capability whose two values coincide is not, on its own, responsible for the observed gain. The control is a complement set, so its composition depends on how often the capability is invoked: for a capability used on a small fraction of questions the control approximates the model’s overall gain, whereas for one used on the majority of questions the control is a small and atypical remainder.

A.1 Tool-Call Volume and Engagement

Two quantities characterize how heavily a model uses the tools, and they vary independently: the number of calls a question costs, and the fraction of questions answered with no call. Table 4 reports them per model, and Figure 5 resolves them by domain.

Volume and engagement.

Engagement varies with model scale within a family but not across families. The smaller models leave a substantial fraction of questions untouched (Qwen3-VL-8B 28.9%28.9\%, GPT-6 Luna 25.3%25.3\%), whereas the larger models rarely do (6.2%6.2\%, 4.8%4.8\% and 2.6%2.6\%). Call volume does not order the models by accuracy: GPT-6 Luna issues the fewest calls per question of the five and attains higher accuracy than either Qwen model in Table 1. By domain, grounded perception engages all five models on nearly every question, while spatial reasoning and general VQA and hallucination account for most of the unengaged questions in the smaller models.

Reliability and context cost.

Fewer than 1%1\% of calls return a tool error for any model, so execution reliability is not a limiting factor. Repeated calls, defined as byte-identical invocations within one rollout, are more frequent than errors but remain a small fraction of traffic and do not scale with model size. The dominant cost is context: a rollout occupies between 88 and 1414 transcript turns, between two and 3.53.5 of which are Environment Updates, one emitted at the start and one after each call.

A.2 Distribution of Tool Calls

Aggregate distribution.

Visual Grounding accounts for the largest share of calls in all five models, ranging from 45%45\% for GPT-6 Sol to 63%63\% for Qwen3-VL-32B. The models differ mainly in the second-ranked capability. GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Astra allocate 20%20\% and 18%18\% of their calls to Zoom-in, against 55–9%9\% for the other models, corresponding to a ground-then-inspect pattern. The GPT-6 models allocate a larger share to web retrieval (17%17\% to Text Search for Luna, 13%13\% for Sol, and 9%9\% for Astra), concentrated in the visual search and deep research domain. Depth Estimation, Camera Trajectory and the Python Coding Agent are small in aggregate and concentrated in the spatial reasoning datasets.

Distribution by domain.

Figure 7 resolves the same budget by domain. Grounded perception is dominated by Visual Grounding for every model, at 9090–94%94\% of domain calls, with the exception of GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Astra, which allocate roughly a quarter of their calls in that domain to Zoom-in. Visual search and deep research is the only domain in which the three web capabilities dominate. Spatial reasoning is the one domain in which four capabilities carry comparable load, combining grounding, camera trajectory, depth and the coding agent, and general VQA and hallucination divides between grounding and inspection.

A.3 Effect of Tool Use on Accuracy

Aggregate effect.

All five models improve under OpenVLHarness, by +6.2+6.2 (GPT-6 Astra) to +10.1+10.1 (Qwen3-VL-8B) points. The net figure is the balance of two considerably larger flows: between 2,3362{,}336 and 4,6494{,}649 questions per model are corrected, while between 700700 and 2,1462{,}146 are degraded. Normalizing by the tool calls spent, the cost of a net corrected question ranges from 11.711.7 calls (GPT-6 Luna) to 28.128.1 calls (Qwen3-VL-32B), the latter combining the highest call volume with one of the smaller gains.

Null control.

On questions where the agent issued no tool call, OpenVLHarness reduces to the base model with a longer system prompt, so the expected paired difference is zero. The measured values are −0.2-0.2 (GPT-6 Sol), −0.5-0.5 (GPT-6 Luna), −1.6-1.6 (Qwen3-VL-32B) and −1.8-1.8 (Qwen3-VL-8B) points, and +1.8+1.8 for GPT-6 Astra, which leaves only 2.6%2.6\% of questions without a call, so its value rests on 614614 questions. The proximity to zero supports the interpretation of the remaining differences as effects of tool use rather than of the prompt or the evaluation protocol, and the two larger negative values, both from the Qwen3-VL models, indicate a small cost to carrying the tool interface when it is not used.

Per-capability effects.

Figure 8 reports, for each capability and model, the paired difference on the questions that invoked it. Table 6 gives the underlying counts, the share of questions each capability was invoked on, the accuracies of both arms, and the control, that is the same difference on the questions that did not invoke the capability. The two retrieval capabilities exhibit the largest separation from their controls in every model: rows invoking Image Search improve by 18.918.9 to 27.127.1 points, while the corresponding control values lie between −0.6-0.6 and +6.6+6.6. Visual Grounding is the dominant factor for the smaller models — Qwen3-VL-8B improves by 14.314.3 points on rows that ground and declines by 20.120.1 points on rows that do not — and flattens for the larger models, which invoke it on nearly all questions. Camera Trajectory is positive for all five models. Depth Estimation, OCR, Zoom-in and the Python Coding Agent are at or below their controls, apart from Zoom-in for GPT-6 Luna (+11.9+11.9 against +8.6+8.6) and GPT-6 Astra (+9.4+9.4 against +5.2+5.2), which is consistent with their being invoked on the questions a model cannot resolve from the image alone rather than with their being ineffective in isolation.

A.4 Capability Composition

Composition across capabilities.

Rollouts frequently combine several capabilities rather than invoking one in isolation. Counting the number of distinct capabilities per rollout, among engaged rollouts 31.9%31.9\% (Qwen3-VL-32B), 26.8%26.8\% (GPT-6 Sol) and 26.0%26.0\% (GPT-6 Astra) invoke two or more, against 20.7%20.7\% and 11.6%11.6\% for the smaller models, and the longest rollouts combine four or five. Combinations that cross capability families are rarer, 44–16%16\% of engaged rollouts, and consist almost entirely of a perception capability followed by the Python Coding Agent: ground or measure first, then compute over the resulting quantities. This is the pattern rewarded by the counting, grounding and spatial datasets, and it is not expressible in a harness that exposes a single capability.

Appendix B Additional Results and Analysis

This section reports results with additional backbones (GPT-5, GPT-6 Sol, and Kimi K3), gives details of the ablation in Table 3, compares OpenVLHarness with training-based harnesses, analyzes grounded perception across object counts, extends the visual search and deep research results to 1111 information-seeking benchmarks, and tests whether additional reasoning can replace the harness.

B.1 Additional Backbones

Table 7 evaluates OpenVLHarness with GPT-5 (OpenAI, 2025b), with GPT-6 Sol (OpenAI, 2026), and with Kimi K3 (Team et al., 2026), an open-weight mixture-of-experts model with native visual understanding, on the same 2222 datasets as Table 1, using the same tools, memory, prompts, and scoring. With GPT-6 Sol, OpenVLHarness improves every one of the 2222 benchmarks, raising the average from 52.752.7 to 64.364.3.

B.2 Ablation Study Details

The ablation in Table 3 isolates the contribution of each harness component by building a strict superset ladder: every rung adds exactly one mechanism to the one below it, so the gap between adjacent rungs measures that mechanism’s marginal value.

Variants.

The five rungs are:

  1. 1.

    Baseline (no tool). The backbone model prompted directly with the question image and no tool access, establishing the no-harness floor.

  2. 2.

    + Tool. The nine tools are available, but their payloads arrive as raw dumps, their schema is cut to a minimal signature (name, argument names and types, one clause each), and nothing persists between turns: no environment updates, no image labels, no data bindings, no URL references. Tool-generated images are replaced by a short stub.

  3. 3.

    + Capability layer. Adds the capability layer of Sec. 2.1: each tool’s raw payload is replaced by a per-tool post-processor that condenses it into a concise, model-readable summary (e.g. grounding boxes on a 0–1000 grid, reranked search results with inline citations, depth/zoom captions), and the full tool schema is restored so the model is told when to reach for each tool and how to phrase its arguments. No memory is present—nothing is carried across turns.

  4. 4.

    + Textual memory. Adds every memory mechanism that is addressed by a text handle: per-turn Environment Updates that re-advertise all live state, webpage_url_N references that let the agent revisit a URL, and out-of-context data bindings that the Python Coding Agent can read as typed variables. Tool-generated images are replaced by a VLM-written text description (up to 160 tokens) conditioned on the original question. Image references remain absent: tool-produced images cannot be named, stored, or passed to a later tool call.

  5. 5.

    OpenVLHarness (full). Adds multimodal image memory: every tool-produced image is labeled (tool_generated_image_N), deduplicated by content, and kept addressable. The model selects which image to pass to each tool call by its identifier, enabling compositions such as grounding →\to zoom →\to OCR →\to search.

Implementation.

All five variants share the same nine-tool toolset, backbone weights, and decoding configuration (temperature 0.70.7, top-pp 0.80.8, top-kk 2020, repetition penalty 1.01.0, presence penalty 1.51.5, up to 12,80012{,}800 generated tokens per turn, 1515 tool-calling iterations, 168168K-token context cap). They differ only in the ablation preset applied to the memory stack: a configuration block that switches individual mechanisms (environment updates, image identifiers, per-tool post-processors, data bindings, URL references) on or off. Each preset is a strict superset of the one below it, validated at initialization so a typo fails the run rather than silently selecting the wrong baseline. Table 8 summarizes the knob settings for each variant.

Evaluation setup.

Each variant is evaluated on 22 datasets spanning all four domains in Table 1. For efficiency, datasets with more than 500 samples are subsampled to 500 examples with a fixed random seed (4242) shared across all variants, so every rung sees exactly the same instances. All reported numbers are means of three independent runs with different sampling seeds. Domain averages in Table 3 are macro-averages over the datasets in each domain.

B.3 Training-Based Baselines

Table 9 compares OpenVLHarness with the three training-based harnesses on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, the base model all three are fine-tuned from (setup in Appendix G.2). Averaged over the 2222 datasets, OpenVLHarness reaches 33.4533.45, ahead of PixelReasoner (28.0228.02), AdaReasoner (25.2925.29), and DeepEyesV2 (25.0225.02), without updating any weights.

Where training helps and where it does not.

The margin is largest on grounded perception (23.0523.05 vs. at most 10.4110.41) and on visual search and deep research (19.9119.91 vs. at most 15.5915.59). The training-based harnesses are optimized for a fixed tool set and answer style: they rarely produce the dense, well-formed box lists that FSCD and OdinW require, and none of them retrieves web evidence in our setup, so knowledge-intensive search questions fall back on the 7B model’s parametric knowledge. On general VQA and hallucination and on spatial reasoning, which resemble their training distributions, the gap narrows (50.5850.58 vs. 49.3249.32 and 39.5439.54 vs. 39.3739.37), and the trained models are best on a few perception-centric datasets such as RealWorldQA and V*, where PixelReasoner’s learned zoom-in behavior pays off. Training a model into one tool protocol thus helps in-distribution but transfers poorly, whereas a training-free harness can cover all four domains with the same weights.

The backbone as orchestrator.

Absolute scores with OpenVLHarness on Qwen2.5-VL-7B are well below those on Qwen3-VL (Table 1). Because the harness relies on the backbone to plan tool calls and to follow output conventions, a weaker orchestrator limits its benefit; on OdinW-13-All, for example, OpenVLHarness reaches only 7.807.80 AP with Qwen2.5-VL-7B versus 50.4050.40 with Qwen3-VL-8B. The harness therefore benefits directly from stronger backbones, with no retraining when a new backbone is adopted.

B.4 Grounded Perception Across Object Counts

Most counting and grounding benchmarks rarely test models at high object counts, which can make headline scores misleading. To make this concrete, we bin every sample of widely used counting and grounding datasets by its number of target objects (Figures 9 and 10). For counting, TallyQA (Acharya et al., 2019), CountBenchQA (Paiss et al., 2023), and PixmoCount place essentially all samples at ten or fewer objects; only FSC-147 and FSCD-LVIS contribute meaningful mass above 5050 objects. Grounding is even more skewed: referring-expression datasets such as RefCOCO/+/g (Kazemzadeh et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2016; Mao et al., 2016), Ref-L4 (Chen et al., 2024a), and GroundingME (Li et al., 2025a) ground exactly one target per sample, and detection-style benchmarks such as OdinW-13 and LVIS are dominated by a single object per image (97%97\% and 86%86\% of samples in the 00–11 bucket). Dense, many-object grounding appears only in the FSCD variants. This is why our suite includes FSC-147, FSCD-147, and FSCD-LVIS, and why we break their results down by object count below.

Results by object count.

Table 10 breaks down FSC-147 and FSCD-LVIS by the number of ground-truth objects, using the bins defined above. On FSC-147, OpenVLHarness improves exact-match accuracy in every bucket, with the largest gains between 1111 and 5050 objects (e.g., 5.0→32.95.0\to 32.9 at 8B for 2121–5050), where the base models’ accuracy collapses. On FSCD-LVIS, where every image has at least 2121 instances, the base models recover almost none of the instances (F1 ≤12.5\leq 12.5), whereas OpenVLHarness reaches F1 above 5656 up to 100100 instances and around 4141 beyond. Accuracy nevertheless falls steeply with count for every configuration: above 100100 objects exact counting remains essentially unsolved, confirming that the high-count regime is where the most headroom lies.

Additional metrics and benchmarks.

Table 11 reports complementary counting metrics and an additional grounding benchmark. OpenVLHarness lowers the mean absolute error on FSC-147 and raises CountQA relative accuracy, showing that it also reduces large miscounts rather than only fixing near misses. On LVIS (federated val), which queries both present and absent categories over 1,2031{,}203 classes, OpenVLHarness more than doubles AP at both scales (18.1→45.218.1\to 45.2 at 8B and 22.9→45.522.9\to 45.5 at 32B).

B.5 Extended Visual Search and Deep Research Results

Table 12 extends the search results to 1111 information-seeking benchmarks, including five that are not in Table 1. The agent workflow improves every backbone: the average across the 1111 benchmarks rises from 13.7413.74 to 29.0529.05 for Qwen3-VL-8B, from 19.2119.21 to 34.6134.61 for Qwen3-VL-32B, and from 31.5831.58 to 41.8041.80 for GPT-5. Gains are largest for the open models, whose parametric knowledge is most limited; GPT-5’s direct-inference accuracy is additionally depressed by refusals on identity queries (Appendix D.2). With the harness, Qwen3-VL-32B surpasses direct GPT-5 on average (34.6134.61 vs. 31.5831.58).

B.6 Reasoning-Effort Study: Setup and Full Results

OpenVLHarness answers a question over several model calls, and each call carries tool outputs and memory, so it spends more model tokens per question than prompting the base model directly. This raises the question of whether the harness helps simply by spending more compute: a reasoning model given a larger token budget might recover the gain by reasoning for longer. GPT-6 Luna exposes a reasoning-effort setting, which lets us test this directly by raising the effort of every method, including OpenVLHarness. Section 3.3 and Figure 1c summarize the results. Table 13 reports domain averages and costs, Table 14 the tokens per question behind the costs, Table 15 how often Codex executes code, and Table 16 the per-benchmark scores.

Setup.

We run Base, Codex, Visual Sketchpad, and OpenVLHarness with GPT-6 Luna at five reasoning-effort settings (low, medium, high, xhigh, and max) on the full evaluation splits of all 2222 benchmarks of Table 1, that is, 26,22926{,}229 questions per setting and 524,580524{,}580 in total. Each method keeps its configuration from Table 1 and Appendix G.1, and the medium-effort setting is the configuration reported in Table 1. Apart from the effort, only two settings change. First, Base, Visual Sketchpad, and OpenVLHarness may produce up to 16,00016{,}000 output tokens per model call, raised to 64,00064{,}000 at max effort so that reasoning is not truncated; Codex uses its own default limit. Second, GPT-6 Luna accepts max effort only through the Responses API, so Base switches to that API at max effort; OpenVLHarness and Codex use it at every setting, and the Chat Completions requests of Visual Sketchpad are translated to it at every setting. The Python Coding Agent of OpenVLHarness uses the same reasoning effort as the orchestrator. Codex is the Codex CLI agent (OpenAI, 2025a, see Appendix G.1): every question runs in a fresh session with the image attached and web search disabled to prevent the model from searching the web for the benchmark’s gold answer, and model-written code executes in a read-only sandbox enforced with Landlock and seccomp. All settings were run on the Flex service tier.

Cost is the GPT-6 Luna API bill for model tokens: uncached input, cache reads and writes, and output, including hidden reasoning tokens. We price all settings at Standard-tier rates; the Flex tier halves every price and leaves cost ratios unchanged. Costs exclude tool execution (e.g., SAM 3, OCR, and search APIs) and judging, and are averaged over the 2222 benchmarks in the same way as the scores. Scoring follows Table 1; on the search benchmarks, every setting is scored with the GPT-4o judge used in that table. A question whose requests fail on every retry counts as incorrect; this occurred for 134134 of the 524,580524{,}580 questions (marked † in Table 16).
